title: California announces minimum wage increase as governor taunts Trump
summary: Gavin Newsom says new pay floor of $17.40, set to become highest of any US state, will go into effect on 1 January
body: California governor Gavin Newsom announced that the state’s minimum wage will rise to $17.40 next year, a ay floor set to become the highest of any US state. The pay bump will go into effect starting 1 January, Newsom announced on Friday. The state’s current minimum rate is $16.90. In a news release, Newsom touted the move as a salve for working families amid high living costs and took a jab at the Trump administration. “For years, Donald Trump and Republicans have blocked efforts to raise the federal minimum wage while handing tax breaks to billionaires and big corporations,” Newsom said. The federal minimum wage was last increased during George W Bush’s presidency, when it rose from $6.55 to $7.25. Opponents of a federal increase fear adverse effects to the labor market such as job losses. “California has chosen a different path – one that rewards work, grows the economy and puts working families first. We believe if you work hard, you deserve a decent paycheck. They think $7.25 an hour is enough. We don’t,” Newsom said. Thirty states in addition to Washington DC have set wage rates above the federal minimum. The state of Washington will trail close behind California in 2027 with a minimum wage of $17.13, according to data from the Department of Labor. In New York City and three nearby counties, the minimum wage is $17. Since Newsom took the gubernatorial seat in 2019, the state’s minimum wage has grown from $12, according to his office. Still, for a family of two working adults and two children in California, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) estimate each adult must earn $36.38 to cover food, childcare, healthcare, housing and transportation, among other basic necessities. Cost-of-living concerns have been at the forefront of the upcoming midterm elections. The Trump administration has faced blowback over the protracted war with Iran that has led to a surge in gas prices across the nation. In California, a state that relies on a reduced emission type of gasoline, fuel prices topped $6 per gallon in recent months.

title: EU to hold urgent meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday over Ceuta crisis
summary: Divisions remain in the bloc over mass crossing of migrants into Spanish territory in north Africa
body: The EU is to hold an urgent meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday amid continued divisions in the bloc over the arrival of more than 50,000 migrants in the Spanish territory of Ceuta in north Africa. The decision was taken by officials representing EU member states and Frontex border agency experts at what was described as a “sobering” meeting on Saturday. Spain confirmed at least 67 people had died in the attempted crossing. Some drowned, while others were crushed as they tried to cross a breakwater barrier. The decision to call a summit of ministers was unanimous as EU leaders seek to heal divisions in the bloc and restore a unified approach to migration. Spain said migrant crossings into Ceuta had stopped overnight, as police began installing a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier off its border ‌with Morocco. Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, said on Saturday: “I have been in touch with the Spanish prime minister and [we are] providing what help we can.” Italy and Denmark, with some support from Poland and Sweden, used the meeting on Saturday to criticise Spain for what had happened. In a furious letter on Saturday, Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez hit out against “fake news” and “disinformation”, pointing out that “virtually all” migrants had been returned to Morocco after the army intervened on Friday, “preventing any unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe”. It is understood suspected Russian attempts to spread disinformation to sow dissent within the EU was also discussed at the meeting on Saturday. There is frustration in Spain that previous incidents of this scale, such as mass arrival of migrants on the border of Belarus and Poland or Russia and Finland, were labelled as “hybrid attacks” , and met with solidarity from the rest of the EU. Although more than 48,000 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco by 6pm on Friday, the influx triggered a political crisis for the Madrid government and led some fellow EU countries to call for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Juan Jesús Vivas, the president of Ceuta, said that while many people had returned to Morocco, not all those who had crossed into the city had left. “We’re not back to normal because there are several thousand people who need to be returned, and there is still an atmosphere marked by unease and concern,” he said. He also called for “all the security measures deployed” in Ceuta to remain in place to guarantee the safety of the population. Sánchez asked for the meeting after what appeared to be a breakdown of EU unity on external border policy, with Italy attacking Spain. Italy announced on Friday evening that it would suspend its Schengen arrangements with Spain for a month, even though Ceuta – and Spain’s other north African territory, Melilla – are subject to special Schengen rules that prevent onward movement within the zone. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now-closed scheme to regularise the status of more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”. Sánchez was forthright in a letter sent to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Council president, António Costa, and Micheál Martin, the prime minister of Ireland, which holds the EU presidency. Sánchez said that while most EU countries had expressed support and solidarity over events in Ceuta, others had chosen to attack Spain. “Such an attitude – driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest – is … contrary to European law, humanitarian law and the principles of solidarity that bind us together,” he said. In a pointed rebuke to Italy, he noted that Spain was “according to Frontex, one of the least porous external borders of the European Union, with a number of irregular entries that is half that recorded, for example, in Italy in recent years (2021–26)”. Senior EU officials met on Saturday in a “political crisis response team” convened by Ireland’s presidency. Ireland’s prime minister, Micheál Martin, said on Saturday that, as the holders of the EU presidency, “Ireland will convene a meeting on Tuesday of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council, chaired by Jim O’Callaghan [justice minister], to discuss developments in Ceuta. “We remain in close contact with all member states and the institutions and continue to monitor the situation,” he said in a social media post. O’Callaghan, who is leading the meetings on behalf of the EU, said he had been in touch with Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, to express his solidarity and support. In remarks that appeared to respond to Sánchez’s criticisms, von der Leyen said she welcomed his suggestion of a video conference “to take stock of what has happened”, adding: “Fighting illegal migration requires solidarity and a united European response.” France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said his country would not be seeking Spain’s suspension from Schengen rules. “It’s absolutely not on the table,” he said on Saturday. “We have great cooperation with Spain.” Many of the remaining people who crossed into Ceuta returned to Morocco on Saturday morning amid a reinforced Spanish police and military presence. “We hope to go to Europe to work and earn a living – that’s it,” Souleil Boyan, a 19-year-old from Senegal, told Agence France-Presse outside a migrant centre in Ceuta where dozens of other people from sub-Saharan Africa were waiting for officials. “We all know that in Africa there isn’t much opportunity,” he added. The Spanish government said in a statement on Saturday that the situation in Ceuta remained calm and quiet. It said containment barriers were being installed at the Tarajal beach breakwater, including a 500-metre-long inflatable barrier and a line of anchored buoys. This week’s mass crossing dwarfs the last similar event in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over two days. That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed the territory to Morocco and Mauritania. That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara, a move that caused a rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group. Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria. The Spanish government has attributed the latest influx to “human-trafficking mafias” that have taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta or Melilla could not be summarily returned under special rules. But some migration experts have expressed doubts about that explanation. Mauricio Valiente, the director general of the Spanish Refugee Aid Commission, said the route into Ceuta was very different from the Atlantic route from Africa to the Canary Islands, which is often operated by people smugglers. “Unlike what happens in the Canary Islands, these aren’t people who have to get into a small boat,” he told elDiario.es. “This is a matter of being just metres from a land border, jumping into the sea and trying to get around a breakwater, which makes it much easier to do, even with all the risks.” Valiente said there had been a steady increase in arrivals to Ceuta this year, even before the supreme court ruling. “The causes are complex, and there are surely many reasons,” he said. “But to simplify it by referencing the court ruling or organised crime – to say there’s a direct cause-and-effect relationship – is completely unfounded.” Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, visited Ceuta on Saturday and said he had spoken to migrants there. “I have spoken to a number of them who made it quite clear they intend to make it to Britain,” he said.

title: Upheaval in Maine and another 100-day campaign - can Democrats pull it off?
summary: Troy Jackson gained the party nomination for Senate, but now he needs to consolidate support to take on Susan Collins
body: Troy Jackson is ready to move on. In fewer than 100 days, the new Democratic nominee has to convince Maine voters to send him to the US Senate – and he’s trying to do it without dwelling on Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after accusations of rape, which he denies. “The movement represented in this room did not just begin two weeks ago,” said Jackson, a progressive lumberjack and former state lawmaker who won nearly all the delegates at a hastily organized special convention last Saturday. “I’ve always known that your trust has to be earned.” On stage, no one mentioned Platner by name, but the fallout from the oyster farmer’s campaign collapse hung over the room. He had ridden an anti‑establishment wave before crashing under a series of scandals – which included problematic online posts, a tattoo resembling a Nazi symbol and allegations of abusive behavior in past relationships. Jackson, who previously launched an unsuccessful bid for governor this year, now faces a compressed timeline to build the same momentum his predecessor generated against Susan Collins, the moderate Republican who has weathered every challenger during her three decades in the Senate. Maine is central to Democrats’ effort to pick up the four seats they need to regain control of the upper chamber in the midterms. But some in the party worry that Jackson faces a steep climb in a short window. “He won an interparty fight – which is nothing like the fight he’s got ahead of him,” said Lynn Bromley, a former Democratic state senator. “He’s going to have to build a statewide coalition. That’s a whole different process.” “I would say Jackson has momentum, but I would also say momentum isn’t the same thing as trust,” she added. Who Jackson needs to win Jackson quickly emerged as the natural heir to Platner’s anti‑oligarchy message. More than 17,000 voters turned out for the county‑level delegate elections, and by the time the roughly 500 selected delegates arrived in Bangor, most had already pledged to support Jackson. In a Tuesday interview on political talkshow Morning Joe, Jackson acknowledged that Platner was the more compelling orator, but said his focus now is making sure voters understand the election is about “the movement”, not any one candidate. To win in November, he still has to consolidate Democratic support and reach voters outside Platner’s core supporters. The most crucial demographic for Jackson is 2020 ticket‑splitters in Maine – those who backed Susan Collins for Senate and Joe Biden for president. Back then, Collins ultimately won by nine points, defeating Democrat Sara Gideon, the former state house speaker, despite trailing in most public polls. A Guardian review shows that more municipalities voted for both Biden and Collins than they did for a straight Democratic ticket that year. One of those voters is Wendy Tooth, a physiotherapist in Manchester, who’s been “disappointed” with Collins since her 2020 vote for the incumbent, and particularly since Donald Trump’s re-election. “I wasn’t really a Graham Platner fan,” Tooth, 58, said. “[Collins] doesn’t seem as centrist as she used to be. She seems to go along with a lot of Trump’s policies, which I don’t agree with.” Part of the unenrolled bloc that makes up about a third of voters in the Pine Tree state, Tooth says she needs to see Jackson “work across party lines” – and Collins take firmer positions against the war in Iran and the deadly federal immigration crackdown across the country – before making her decision. Democrats such as Alan Blake of Thomaston say the party must now rally behind Jackson regardless of any concerns about the chaos that has plagued the race so far. “We’re just going to carry Jackson in there because we absolutely need the policies he stands for,” Blake, 74, added. “It’s not drastic to say we’re trying to save democracy here.” And Ellie Gunnoe, 39, a psychiatric nurse practitioner and registered Democrat in New Gloucester, said Jackson – a fifth‑generation logger from Aroostook county – can reach voters across the state as a “working‑class Mainer”. “We just need someone fighting in our corner,” Gunnoe added, noting that the fatal shooting of 26-year-old Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, by an ICE agent in Biddeford, is one of the key motivators pushing her to the ballot box this year. “My husband is Mexican American and is the exact same age and brown, and so it’s just been feeling increasingly unsafe for people like us,” she added. A slice of moderate Democrats who voted for Janet Mills, Maine’s term-limited governor, in the June primary – after she had suspended her campaign but remained on the ballot – are also in play. One of them, Brenda Garrand, 69, of Rockland, said she plans to vote for Jackson even though she doesn’t consider herself a progressive. “I don’t think he’s the best and brightest, I don’t think he is Senate material,” she said. “But we’ve got to have a Senate majority.” Mills, for her part, told a local ABC affiliate this week that Collins is “vulnerable” and “should be defeated”, but did not endorse Jackson directly. Jackson’s run could be buoyed by the anti-Trump animus that’s grown since the financial fallout of the ongoing war. According to a recent New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll, only 39% of likely Maine voters approved of the president’s job performance since he returned to the White House. “Susan Collins keeps telling us everything is just fine. And you know they act like you know we’re idiots. We know it isn’t. We all have eyes,” Jackson said in Bangor. He used his victory to highlight Collins’ votes to confirm the supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh and advance the president’s $70bn bill to guarantee funding for federal immigration enforcement. “Who has she served?” Jackson asked the audience. “She has served Donald Trump. She voted with them 96% of the time.” Meanwhile, Collins has sought to brand Jackson a “Bernie bro”, pointing to his long relationship with Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, and his role leading Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign in Maine. Ronald Schmidt, a politics professor at the University of Southern Maine, said that attack puts the onus on Jackson to “flip that playbook” of being affiliated with an outsider and “link [Collins] to Trump”. But some local Republicans counter that Jackson’s more than two decades as a state legislator, and a failed run for Congress in 2014, mean he lacks Platner’s outsider profile. “He is Maine’s establishment,” said Chuck Ellis, chair of the Cumberland county GOP. “All the appeal of Platner being anti‑establishment is lost when you replace him with a career politician.” The long road ahead, paved with attack ads An ad offensive from conservative Pacs has begun painting Jackson as an extension of Platner, often using footage from their time on the campaign trail when they endorsed each other. After Jackson clinched the nomination on Saturday, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) even pushed out an AI video of Platner morphing into Jackson with the caption: “No tattoo, same crazy.” James Blair, a former White House adviser now leading Trump’s midterm operation, wrote that Jackson carried “all the baggage” of Platner “without the ‘rizz”. And the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) – the top Senate GOP Super Pac, which has pledged more than $40m to the race – is highlighting the many scandals that plagued the unvetted Platner, alongside reporting about Jackson’s alleged fiery temper during his time in the state legislature. “Jackson is like Graham Platner but worse,” the voiceover in a video says. Meanwhile, the Republican National Committee (RNC) quickly cast Jackson’s nomination as illegitimate, drawing a parallel to the 2024 Democratic convention, where Harris became the nominee after delegates originally pledged to Biden backed her following his withdrawal from the race. “This coronation is proof that Democrats are willing to shove socialism down the throats of Maine voters,” spokesperson Kristen Cianci said. Collins told reporters in Casco last weekend that her challenger’s platform economic populism – which includes many of Platner’s policies such as Medicare for All and taxing the ultra-wealthy – is untenable. “It is disturbing for me to hear Troy say that everything should be free, when in fact it’s going to be middle- and low-income taxpayers who are going to be paying the bill,” she said. Jackson’s ground game is also in need of a significant financial boost to compete with Collins’ war chest of more than $11m cash on hand, according to her latest disclosures. As of now, Jackson’s campaign reports he has amassed $2m since he won the nomination. That’s on top of the $1m he raised since he formally entered the Senate race in early July. Perhaps more daunting than the attacks or the finances, however, is the support Collins has built over five terms, and a record of political survival that has been impossible to beat – even when the odds appear to be against her. “She’s an intimidating political presence, and I think people underestimate that,” said Matt Gorman, a Republican strategist. Collins has spent much of the race, and the years leading up to it, underscoring the millions of dollars in federal funding she’s steered to Maine as chair of the powerful Senate appropriations committee. Her campaign spokesperson, Shawn McRoderick, said the senator looks forward to “waging a vigorous, issues‑oriented campaign that will distinguish her record of accomplishment against Troy’s angry soundbites”. In a small state, tangible results are hard to ignore. “I was speaking to a town official from upstate who was able to get fire department money to improve the local volunteer fire department with the help of Collins’ office,” Schmidt recalled. “People who’ve directly been helped by her staff probably will vote for her again in this election, regardless of their party ID.” While antipathy toward the gerontocracy may c…

title: Trump offering early access to online posts in move seen as corruption
summary: Truth Social, where Trump’s account is by far the largest, to offer users early access for up to $100,000 per month
body: Donald Trump is now offering early access to his Truth Social posts in a move that has been seen as corruption benefitting a sitting president. Trump Media and Technology Group officially rolled out its new subscription-based data service on Saturday, giving paying customers faster, real-time access to Truth Social posts from Trump and other high-profile accounts. Called Truth API, the application programming interface is intended to provide businesses with “a direct, licensed, real-time feed of the platform’s most market-moving Truths”, interim CEO Kevin McGurn said in a release announcing the launch. Trading firms and other paying subscribers can now access the posts earlier than other users – for a fee of up to $100,000 per month. The new offering mirrors similar paid data services available on competing social media platforms, though with a particularly steep price tag. However, Truth Social stands apart because its most influential user is Trump, who is also the largest shareholder of the publicly traded parent company, meaning he could personally benefit from the service. Although the announcement does not specifically mention Trump, his @realDonaldTrump account is by far the platform’s largest. He frequently uses it to announce major policy decisions before making them elsewhere. As of Saturday, the account had 13 million followers. Critics argue the service is blatant evidence of market manipulation and insider trading. Trump has repeatedly used Truth Social to reveal significant policy moves with the potential to shift financial markets, including posts involving tariffs and the Iran war. The launch comes just days after Democratic senators Adam Schiff and Elizabeth Warren called on the Securities and Exchange Commission to examine the new service. In a letter dated Tuesday and sent to SEC chair Paul Atkins, the lawmakers urged the agency to investigate whether the company was breaking the law. “This appears to be an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders,” they wrote. Last year, Trump published more than 100 Truth Social posts in a single day while global stock markets tumbled amid concerns that his economic agenda could trigger a “Trumpcession” in the US. His posts about Iran have drawn particular attention because investors remain concerned that rising oil prices could keep inflation elevated and potentially lead the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates. Trump Media’s stock has fallen by more than 70% since the president took office last year, wiping out roughly $6bn (£4.4bn) in shareholder value. Those losses, combined with billions more in investor losses connected to new Trump family cryptocurrency ventures, have come under increased scrutiny after Trump’s annual financial disclosure showed he generated more than $1 billion in revenue last year from the same companies and offerings. On Friday, one day before Truth API’s debut, shares of Trump Media climbed 5.5% to $10.39 shortly before the market closed, reported Forbes. The president’s company has primarily depended on advertising revenue, but the new API service could expand its revenue sources if it proves successful.

title: Trump’s reflecting pool saga: a timeline of failure and finger-pointing
summary: As Jeanine Pirro moves to drop charges, flawed work by Trump-connected contractor emerges as culprit
body: Donald Trump’s Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool saga appears to be winding down after prosecutors dropped vandalism charges against former Olympian David Hearn – but not entirely. On Friday, Trump appointee and US attorney Jeanine Pirro and assistant US attorney Michael ⁠Spence petitioned a judge to dissolve the justice department’s case against Hearn, 67, who had been accused of pool sabotage, and instead blamed the “botched installation” of pool liner materials that caused it peel, and “less than fulsome information” offered by the Department of Interior. “I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, on the Reflecting Pool. I don’t know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM,” the president posted on social media on Saturday. Trump’s attempts to renovate the pool, and the millions he has spent to do so, may endure in memory not only as a warning about the persistence of mother nature during Washington DC’s hot and muggy summer months, but also the perils of the president’s insistence on fast-tracked renovations in advance of a major celebration, in this case America’s 250th year since independence. April 2026 The odyssey begins Trump says he was inspired to undertake the renovation after complaints of a friend visiting from Germany, who he said told him the water in the pool was dark and filthy, and looked disgusting. The administration initiates a no-bid project to seal seams and coat the basin bottom in “American flag blue”. The plan envisioned a one-to-two-week timeline to drain the pool and reseal it. Costs were estimated at $1.5m-$2m. The pool, which holds approximately 4m gallons of water, was previously renovated in 2012, at a cost of $34m, in an effort to improve its floor support system to prevent the pool from sinking. But neither the algae blooms, nor its leaking joints, have ever been resolved. Bypassing the National Park Service, Greenwater Services of Brookfield, Ohio, was selected to install a water-purification system using patented NanoBubble Ozone Technology (NBOT). Federal contracting records reveal that firm’s ultimate owner is the JJ Cafaro Investment Trust, led by John J Cafaro, a Trump donor and a neighbor to Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s “Winter White House”, in Florida. Atlantic Industrial Coatings, the contractor responsible for the lining project, and Mid-America Industrial Coatings, a subcontractor, elected to use two products, Pipeliner 5000 in dark blue and a light blue Rhino 406 primer, for the project. May 2026 Trump faces legal challenges The pool project faces legal challenges from non-profits, which try to block the blue refinishing over historic preservation concerns. Work continues, deadlines are missed and the scope of the work expands. On 7 May, Trump visits the reflecting pool, according to a press release from the White House. His motorcade drives straight over the drained, coated basin of the pool alongside cabinet members Doug Burgum of the interior department and Markwayne Mullin of the homeland security department. Trump says the original gray stone was “never good”, adding: “It never had the color people wanted, but now it’s going to have the great color.” June 2026 Trump blames vandals, Hearn is arrested The pool is refilled with water but reprieve from algae blooms is brief. Maintenance crews apply hydrogen peroxide and the bubble technology to try to stop the takeover. The blue liner begins to peel and bubble. Costs climb to between $14m and $16m. Less than two weeks before America 250 celebrations are set to culminate, and while the pool’s status is in the national limelight, former Olympian David Hearn is arrested and charged with property destruction. Hearn, the only person facing a felony charge over damage to the reflecting pool, pleads not guilty. If convicted, he faces a 10-year prison sentence and a $1,000 fine. Trump says: “We had vandalism. It’s not a lot of damage, but we’ll probably have to let the water out and re-fix it. They went in there with a knife. I was just told by the people over at Parks, five people are arrested, and five people are under investigation right now – and it’s a sad thing.” Early July 2026 Celebrations begin as pool remains political On 2 July, Pirro says National Park Service employees witnessed Hearn “forcefully and violently” pulling at the liner and becoming belligerent when told to stop. Anti-algae and cleanup efforts continue through Independence Day celebrations. Soon after, the pool is drained a second time to clear out fireworks debris and address the peeling coating. 31 July 2026 Trump administration dismisses case against Hearn Prosecutors said they could no longer move forward with the case against Hearn and instead blamed damage to the pool liner as “the result of flawed installation by the contractor”. In a 20-page court filing in DC superior court, prosecutors said they had received information about a “rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration in the weeks surrounding Independence Day 2026”. In the document, the government acknowledged “a rushed and flawed installation process, with repeated failures of the lining during the installation process, and extensive peeling of the lining throughout the Reflecting Pool”. “It was not until after these documents were produced,” Pirro’s office added, that her office “first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by [the interior department]”. As the reflecting pool remains unfinished, and costs remain high, attorneys for Hearn have said the government “owes Mr Hearn an apology” and Pirro has come under fire. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong. The government’s approach was ready, fire, aim,” they said on social media. Conservative commentator Scott Jennings agreed. “The administration looks like a monkey having intimate relations with a football,” Jennings told CNN’s The Source on Friday. But Trump in his Saturday post did not appear to back down. He acknowledged that “there may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!” In a later post accompanied by an unclear video, he said: “Look for yourselves at the VANDALISM that took place at The Reflecting Pool. The material is being cut with a knife or a box cutter, for all to see!”

title: US reporter fighting back after border patrol seized his cellphones
summary: Max Blumenthal says he was singled out at airport after Trump ally Laura Loomer targeted him in online posts
body: When reporter Max Blumenthal went to a cafe in Tehran one night a few weeks ago to upload videos from his reporting on the funeral of Iran’s supreme leader Ali Khamenei, he began seeing social media posts from Trump ally Laura Loomer targeting him, including one that suggested he should be “taken off the plane by US Marshalls when he lands back in the US … [and] detained”. “I began to prepare myself for being harassed on my return,” Blumenthal said. Effectively, that’s what happened, sparking a legal fight that freedom-of-the-press advocates say shows the determination of the Trump administration to crack down on members of the media whose reporting it disagrees with. On 10 July, border patrol agents at Virginia’s Dulles airport flagged Blumenthal, founder of the independent outlet the Grayzone, for a “secondary inspection”. Agents asked him how he had paid for his trip to Iran, whether he knew the people who had hosted him and whether he had plans to return. They asked to see his two phones. He declined to give them the passwords. They seized the phones, but not his laptop or digital cameras. The federal agency returned the cellphones a week later – less than 24 hours after the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee filed an emergency motion in district court seeking their return. The US federal government said they couldn’t get into the phones and returned them, and that therefore the motion was moot. But Blumenthal went back to court on Wednesday and got a judge to agree that the government must prove it – by supplying evidence of who had his phones, when they had them and what they did to them. Federal judge Leonie M Brinkema gave the government 14 days to respond. Blumenthal’s treatment and case pose “serious constitutional problems”, said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation. “The Trump administration is finding any excuse it can to target journalists it dislikes, and border searches are one more play in the playbook.” It is the second case concerning cellphone seizures at US airports to hit federal courts in recent weeks, after another involving an activist against the Atlanta police-training center known as “Cop City” had its first evidentiary hearing. Brinkema cited a recent fourth district ruling that distinguished a basic cellphone search – when the phone’s owner allows an agent to open the phone – from an “advanced” search, during which “equipment, wired or wireless, [is used] to copy and/or analyze the contents of an electronic device”. This is what federal agents sought to do with Blumenthal’s phones. “I believe now under fourth circuit case law, a search warrant would be required for that degree of intrusion into a cellphone,” Brinkema said, according to a transcript of the proceedings. No such warrant was produced for Blumenthal. The incident is also the second recent case involving the federal government apparently seeking to discover the sources of journalists, after its failed attempt to subpoena New York Times reporters. Jenin Younes, president of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, noted that the border patrol agents seized only Blumenthal’s phones. “They didn’t take his laptop or digital camera,” she said. “That suggests they’re interested in contacts, sources, personal communications – maybe even tracking data.” Brinkema mentioned the Times case in Wednesday’s hearing. “[G]iven the fact that this plaintiff is a reporter, this case has particular concern to the court because there’s been so much recently in the ether about attempts by the government to intrude upon a reporter’s right to report,” she said. “And, you know, just recently in New York, we had the issue of the subpoenas that were issued to the New York Times reporters,” she continued. “I don’t think that can be overlooked.” “We want to know what they did with [Blumenthal’s] phones,” Younes said. “We want to make sure the administration recognizes the serious privacy interests at stake in taking anyone’s phones – especially journalists.” The judge suggested that Blumenthal could “probably have an expert take a look at his phones to see if there’s any indication … they were somehow tampered with or accessed in some way”. Blumenthal said he’s “working on that – but it costs a lot”. Younes pointed out that many other US journalists were in Iran to cover Khamenei’s funeral, including mainstream outlets such as CNN and the Times – but there’s been no public disclosure of any other reporter being detained upon returning. The posts by Loomer “raise the specter he’s being targeted for his views, for his journalism. This strengthens the first amendment aspect of his case.” Blumenthal said the views that make him a target include him being a “Jewish anti-Zionist”. Wednesday’s hearing, he said, was positive not just for him. “It has positive consequences for other journalists who have faced or will face this kind of repression, from an administration that isn’t responsive to the rule of law,” he said. At the same time, the information he is seeking may turn into what Younes called “a protracted battle”, since the government’s attorney raised the issue that some of what was done with his phones may be “law enforcement privileged information”. “You explain how this is done, and the individuals who we are trying to get information from are able to ‘beat it’,” he said.

title: ‘Agony and despair’: Nancy Guthrie’s family issues new plea for information on her whereabouts
summary: Police also released notes received from presumed abductors of mother of Today anchor Savannah Guthrie
body: The family of Nancy Guthrie issued a new appeal on Saturday for information on the whereabouts of their missing grandmother, six months after she disappeared from her home in Tucson, Arizona, and a day after local investigators released two purported ransom notes. “Six months ago, someone took her out of her bed in the dead of night. We have lived every moment, every breath, and every heartbeat in agony and despair ever since,” a post on Instagram said. “Every day, we wake up and try to be strong and go on – because that’s what our joyful and resilient Mom taught us to do. But make no mistake – our hearts are in ruins,” the Guthrie family added. Eighty-four-year-old Nancy Guthrie, mother of Today show anchor Savannah Guthrie, disappeared from her home on 1 February. But despite intense national attention and the involvement of the FBI, no suspects have been arrested in connection with her disappearance. On Thursday, NBC News reported that two men who were detained and questioned in the days immediately after Nancy Guthrie vanished had issued a “notice of claim” against the Pima county sheriff, Chris Nanos, and a detective on the case. The Pima county sheriff’s department posted a message saying, “The Guthrie investigation remains active and ongoing,” and later released notes received by news outlets soon after Guthrie disappeared. The first note came from someone who claimed they had Guthrie – and that “she is safe but scared” and would not be released until payment in the form of $4m in bitcoin was received. The second said that she had “perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart related. She is buried in nature now.” The presumed abductors added: “Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this and hope you all can find peace. We are truly sorry.” On Saturday, the family issued a new appeal for information leading to Guthrie’s recovery. “We are begging for help. We are desperate. We need someone to come forward. Someone knows something. Someone suspects something. Someone recognizes the writing in the ransom demand notes,” it read. “Please. Bring her home,” the appeal concluded.

title: EU offered Spain support ‘from first moment’ of Ceuta crisis, says von der Leyen, after Sánchez hits out – Europe live
summary: ‘Not a single person reached mainland Spain or rest of EU,’ says European Commission president, after Spanish PM condemned ‘selfish, polarising’ reaction of some countries
body: As EU officials meet to discuss a joint response to irregular arrivals in Ceuta, it is worth remembering that the Spanish prime minister’s ire appears to be directed at Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, who has reacted by closing the Schengen border with Spain despite repeated statements that virtually all the arrivals have returned. On Friday evening, Pedro Sánchez underlined Spain’s efforts at stemming migration by publishing a league table, based on Frontex figures, of irregular arrivals in the EU. In a post on X, he wrote: Solidarity and empathy are optional. Respect for European treaties and data is not. Number of irregular entries between 2021 and 2026 according to Frontex: Via Italy: 478,600 Via the Western Balkans: 340,600 Via Greece: 259,800 Via Spain: 234,760 Via the eastern border: 48,000 This is not the time to divide. It is the time to continue building a strong and united EU. In the past, the EU has called events like Ceuta a “hybrid attack” with “instrumentalisation” of migration for political purposes, as has occurred on the border between Belarus and Poland and Russia and Finland. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said she welcomed calls from leaders for a meeting to “take stock of what has happened” in Ceuta, but maintained that the EU had offered help to Spain “from the first moment”. Her remarks were likely a response to criticism from the Spanish prime minister, who accused Europe of providing “little support” in dealing with the border crisis and called for an emergency meeting of EU interior ministers to address the situation. In a post on X, Von der Leyen said: The good news is that the vast majority of those who arrived illegally have returned to Morocco, due to the effective work of Spanish and Moroccan law enforcement. Not a single person reached mainland Spain or the rest of the EU. This shows why the control of our European borders matters. We have a strong system in place. But it needs to be further strengthened.” Here are some charts and maps put together by our graphic artist Chris Watson illustrating the extent of the wildfires in France and Spain and the areas they have burned: The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has defended her position on the Ceuta border crisis, saying it highlighted the urgent need for a coordinated European response to irregular migration. Italy has temporarily suspended its free-travel Schengen arrangements with Spain by sea and air, claiming it was necessary to safeguard the security of its citizens. Random checks were being carried out today at airports and seaports on travellers arriving from Spain, according to the Spanish EFE news agency. At Rome’s Fiumicino airport, checks were being conducted on flights arriving from Madrid, Barcelona, and Malaga, EFE reported. In a post on X, Meloni said: The images coming out of Ceuta have demonstrated once again just how urgent a European response to illegal immigration is. For this reason, Italy, together with Denmark, has spearheaded a letter signed by 22 European Union member states, calling for joint action to strengthen external borders, tackle irregular migration, combat human traffickers, make returns more effective and eliminate any factors that might encourage further illegal entries. This is an important signal: the position that Italy has long advocated is now shared by an ever-increasing number of European nations. The defence of the Union’s external borders is not in the interest of a single nation. It is a shared responsibility of Europe. Her statement came after the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, accused some EU countries, including Italy, of reacting to the crisis in a “selfish, polarising” manner. He said calls for Spain to be suspended from the EU’s Schengen zone were “driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest” (see post at 10:34). The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Saturday that France would not seek Spain’s suspension from the EU’s Schengen rules, after tens of thousands of people entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in north Africa from Morocco, AFP reports. “Spain does not need to leave the Schengen zone. It’s absolutely not on the table. We have great cooperation with Spain,” he told reporters. On Friday, Italy said it was suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain for a month. The framework allows for visa-free movement between borders. Nuñez said France had stepped up controls at its southern border with Spain, but stressed: “We are not asking for Spain’s suspension from Schengen.” Earlier on Saturday (see post from 10.34 BST), the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, hit back at some EU countries for what he described as their “selfish, polarising and illegal reaction” to the mass border crossings at Ceuta, as he thanked Morocco for its help in dealing with the crisis. The death toll from Russia’s overnight drone and missile attack on Ukraine has now risen to 10 (see post from 09.37 BST) The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, reiterated his call for more air defence support for Ukraine on the Telegram messaging app. “Every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives of our people. And every night without them results in more casualties,” he wrote. The Guardian’s Deborah Cole has written this photo essay about what has been uncovered by the low river levels caused by Europe’s record heat. The Paks nuclear power plant in Hungary, which generates nearly half of the country’s electricity, could be shut down as soon as this weekend amid record-low levels on the Danube River, ⁠the country’s prime minister, Péter Magyar, said on Saturday, Reuters reports. The plant’s Russian-made reactors are operating at just a quarter of their combined 2GW capacity and were expected to be powered down completely for the first ⁠time in 44 years next week amid a further projected decline in water levels. The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he has spoken to his Spanish counterpart, Pedro Sánchez, and offered “what help we can” after more than 50,000 people crossed the border of the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco. PA Media reports that Burnham was asked for his response to the crisis as he attended a rally on Saturday after Labour’s victory in the byelection for the Greater Manchester mayoralty. He told reporters: “I have been in touch with the Spanish prime minister and [we are] providing what help we can.” In other news, Hamburg’s Pride parade, one of Germany’s biggest, has begun with increased security a week after a fatal extremist attack near Berlin’s Pride festival. Organisers expect about 250,000 people to attend the event in Germany’s second-largest city, while police said roughly twice as many officers as last year would be deployed to protect the parade. Here are some early pictures on the newswires from Hamburg: Meanwhile, in another development on the war in Ukraine, Russia’s state-owned nuclear power operator, Rosatom, said Ukrainian drones had sunk a Russian-owned container ship in the Black Sea, forcing its 17-member crew to abandon the vessel. It issued a statement on its Telegram channel of the incident, according to AFP, but it no longer appears on the app (although it has been reported by Russia’s Interfax news agency). AFP reported Rosatom as saying at least two Ukrainian drones struck the “Yanina” cargo vessel last night as it sailed near the Russian port of Novorossiysk. The ship, operated by Rosatom’s shipping subsidiary FESCO, was carrying civilian goods including frozen food and construction materials, Rosatom said. “The ship’s crew abandoned the ship in an organised and coordinated manner after it began to sink. All 17 crew members have been rescued,” Rosatom said in its statement on Telegram, according to AFP. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, confirmed the report, saying the container ship was subject to sanctions. “Thanks to the precision of our defence forces, it was sent to the bottom,” he said. An emergency meeting of EU officials will take place at 2pm today to discuss any further responses to the migration crisis in Ceuta. It comes after Spanish prime minister confirmed “virtually all” the irregular migrants had been returned “preventing any unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe”. However he has asked for the meeting following what appears to be a breakdown of EU unity on external border policy with Italy attacking Spain. Irish justice minister Jim O’Callaghan who is leading as part of Ireland’s EU presidency said he has convened the meeting of the EU integrated political crisis response [IPCR] mechanism and a meeting of EU ambassadors on Monday. The meeting is designed to help member states make clear responses using expert opinion. It is also expected to respond to Spain prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s call for an extraordinary meeting of EU ministers of interior following what he sees as political weaponisation of the crisis. In a strongly worded letter he reminded EU leaders, who have used the crisis to attack Spain, how the EU-wide migration policy has enabled the country “to reduce irregular arrivals through our territory dramatically, making Spain the second most secure external border in the EU, despite being the only Member State with a land border with Africa.”. In a sideswipe at Giorgia Meloni who said it was prepared to “take extraordinary measures” to control its border, Sánchez also noted how it came to the assistance, as called for by the EU migration policy, to Italy. “This successful policy has also allowed us to assist other Member States when they faced similar crises, like when we hosted several of the migrants that arrived to Eastern Europe through Belarus in 2021 and to Lampedusa in 2023,” he said. He said he has asked for the interior ministers’ meeting “as a matter of urgency” so that they can “establish a common response to situations of this kind” and reaffirm that “security of our external borders is a share…

title: Trump vows to push $1.8bn slush fund as Senate committee set to reconsider AG nomination
summary: After declaring ‘anti-weaponization’ fund ‘dead’, Trump reverses and says he’ll revive it despite Senate opposition
body: The US Senate judiciary committee has scheduled a meeting early next week to consider Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, as Donald Trump promised to revive the controversial $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” fund. The meeting, set for Tuesday, comes as Blanche’s confirmation has stalled over a dispute between the president and outgoing Republican senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, who are seeking written confirmation that the justice department would not establish the proposed fund. A spokesperson for the committee said in a statement that Chuck Grassley, committee chair and Iowa Republican, “wants Todd Blanche’s nomination to be successful”. “Grassley would like to see Blanche confirmed before the August recess as he has an excellent record restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe,” the statement added. Opponents of the president consider it a slush fund to compensate political allies for political lawfare; supporters say it is a vehicle to compensate individuals who claim they were wrongfully targeted by the government more broadly. “It is dead, but I wish ⁠it weren’t, to be honest with you. I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused,” Trump had said during a cabinet meeting on Friday. “I’d like to ⁠see them compensated for the pain.” At the cabinet meeting on Friday, Trump urged Republican senators to confirm Blanche and warned that they “will never get anybody like him” and repeated a claim that Cornyn was blocking Blanche because Trump had endorsed Cornyn’s Republican primary challenger Ken Paxton. “I’d be upset also,” ‌Trump said. “I fully understand it. He shouldn’t be that way. I shouldn’t be that way.“ Trump then slammed Cornyn and Tillis in a post on Truth Social on Saturday, claiming that both were upset because he had not endorsed them. Trump threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination, keep him on as acting attorney general and “push hard” for anti-weaponization bill. “Todd Blanche was a voice of reason!” Trump wrote. “It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done.” Blanche, Trump’s former personal attorney, has told senators that the fund was dead, but has so far not agreed to put that in writing. The “anti-weaponization” fund was crafted as part of a ⁠legal settlement between Trump and the justice department to resolve his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS over allegedly mishandling his tax records. Trump wrote that the fund “will not benefit me, but rather the great American Patriots who were hunted down like dogs and whose lives were unfairly and illegally destroyed”. Tillis has said those who attacked law enforcement during the 6 January 2021 riots should still be in prison and should not get a check from the federal government. Cornyn and Tillis also object to an IRS deal that would prevent tax audits of Trump and his associates. Tillis responded on Saturday, saying that despite Trump’s comments that the fund is dead, the president “clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against”. “It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal,” he said on X. “Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday.” The back-and-forth over Blanche’s nomination, which is vigorously opposed by victims of Jeffrey Epstein over his handling of investigative files related to the late sex trafficker, now likely lies with backroom negotiations over the weekend. The same controversy dogged Trump’s original second-term attorney general, Pam Bondi, before she resigned. Cornyn and Tillis were reported to be close to backing Blanche as recently as Thursday. But with just more than two years left in Trump’s second term, Blanche may not need formal Senate confirmation to serve so long as his nomination is pending and not formally rejected or withdrawn.

title: Top mountaineer Nirmal Purja confirmed dead after 11 hit by avalanche in Pakistan
summary: Other members of expedition led by world-renowned climber on Broad Peak have also died, climbing company says
body: A world-renowned Nepali mountaineer and former UK Special Forces member has died after being among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak. Nirmal Purja was killed leading an expedition of 10 other people on the world’s 12th-highest mountain when an avalanche struck at around noon on Thursday. Elite Exped, the company Purja co-founded, said in a statement: “Today it is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak.” “We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive,” it said, without further detail. Purja made history in 2019 after climbing all 14 of the world’s peaks over 8,000 metres in just over six months. He later led the first team to summit K2, the world’s second-highest mountain, in winter. “Records are made to be broken,” the former Gurkha and UKSF member told the Guardian in 2019. “Someone one day will come along and be stronger. People are only limited by their imagination. If you don’t dream, then you won’t do it. Human beings are capable of doing amazing things.” The expedition included five Nepali climbers, as well as US, Pakistani, Omani and Chinese nationals. Another foreign climber was also part of the group, said Karrar Haidri, the vice-president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan. Elite Exped also confirmed the deaths of other expedition members, including his climbing partners and guides, Pur Bahadur Gurung (Yukta), a Nepali citizen, and Nima Sherpa. “Our deepest thoughts, prayers and heartfelt condolences are with their families, friends and loved ones,” the Elite Exped statement said. “No words can erase the pain of this unimaginable loss, and we ask that everyone respects their privacy as they grieve.” On Friday, rescuers had said that four bodies had been found and efforts were under way to retrieve them despite the harsh weather. Among the victims were Nadhira Alharthy, the first Omani to climb Everest, and a US climber, Mallory Geis. Trackers carried by the climbers showed a rapid loss of altitude, suggesting the team had been caught in an avalanche. Purja’s tracker, however, shifted location after the initial rapid descent. The GPS data suggested the avalanche occurred close to 9am local time at 6,579 metres (21,585ft), between camps two and three on the west ridge of the 8,047-metre mountain, the most popular ascent route. The British adventurer Bear Grylls said the news of Purja’s death was “heartbreaking for so many climbers around the world who had a relationship with this remarkable and unique man”. In the 2023 documentary Finding Michael, Purja and Grylls were enlisted to recover the body of Michael Matthews, the youngest Briton to climb Everest, who disappeared on the mountain in 1999. Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of them in the special forces. In 2018, he was awarded an MBE by the queen for his achievements in extreme high-altitude mountaineering. He also drew plaudits for twice risking his life to help others. The first time was while descending from Annapurna, when he led a rescue of fellow climber Chin Wui Kin, who had been separated from an accompanying expedition and left without food, water or oxygen for 40 hours. He later died in hospital. Less than a month later, Purja and his team rescued two climbers from a height of 8,400 metres, sacrificing their own supplementary oxygen to the climbers in need. “For me it’s not about ego,” he previously told the Guardian. “It’s about principles. You can’t call yourself a climber and not help in that situation.” The Prince of Wales said he was “truly saddened to hear of the tragic death” of Purja, adding that he “served with distinction” before “becoming one of the world’s greatest mountaineers”.

title: New York City’s Flatiron building enters new era with $58.5m apartments
summary: Manhattan’s triangular building will open this fall to wealthy residents, with 36 apartments exposing Flatiron’s ‘steel skeleton’
body: New York City’s Flatiron building has had many lives: as a structure seen as a deathtrap; as a nuisance which created a deadly, petticoat-lifting, wind current and, mainly, as a commercial space. Now, the triangular building, a favorite of tourists and locals alike, is entering a new era: as a residential building, where apartments cost up to $58.5m. Completed in 1902, the Flatiron was once derided as a folly, but the Beaux-Arts building is now one of New York’s most admired buildings. Named Flatiron for its resemblance, from above, to a clothes iron, the building’s ornamental brick and terracotta exterior has been hidden behind scaffolding for the best part of seven years. Now, the reimagined Flatiron will open to very wealthy residents later this fall. There are 36 apartments in the building, including some which span entire floors: there’s a double-height lobby, too, a pool, and a games room which will apparently have a billiards table. But for all the shared amenities, the real allure will be the apartments themselves. They have been styled by a venerated New York design firm, which stripped back the interior, exposing some of the Flatiron’s interior “steel skeleton”, the building’s interior steel frame which was cutting edge technology at the time. Images shared with the Guardian show one of the four bedroom, four bathroom apartments in the Flatiron, which features a curved sofa in what the press materials describe as the building’s “prow” – the sharpest angle of the structure. Photos show that there has been a generous application of marble in the bathroom, and equally liberal use of brushed steel in the kitchen. According to the realtor Corcoran’s website, 14 of the apartments in the Flatiron are already in contract. The cheapest, on the third floor, appears to have been bought for $10,950,000: the buyer will get a three bedroom, three bathroom apartment with a not-large open plan kitchen and “great room”. There are also two dressing rooms. The flagship apartment, however, is the one which occupies the entirety of the top floor. In contract for $58.5m, the floorplan of the five bedroom, five bathroom apartment depicts a sauna, two dressing rooms, a dining room and a breakfast room, and a 72ft “great room”. It is unclear who has bid on the apartment. “There’s always hesitation taking on a landmark building like this. But there’s also an advantage. It has an incredibly special character that makes it worth the pain,” Daniel Brodsky, the managing partner of the Brodsky Organization, which owns the building, told the Financial Times in an interview. Brodsky told the Times that Jeff Bezos, the billionaire Amazon founder, had spent more than $100m buying several properties three blocks north of the Flatiron. “There’s a group of wealthy people who want to be in a convenient place; good transportation, the best restaurants in the city, the park … it’s a very easy place to live. You’re surrounded by coolness,” Brodsky said, in what was possibly the first time Bezos’ name has been associated with the term “coolness”. The Flatiron was designed by Daniel Burnham, arguably the hottest architect of its age, and was initially called the Fuller Building. That failed to take off, and ‘Flatiron’ stuck, although pedants might point out that the floorplan of the building is actually a scalene triangle, whereas an actual flatiron would typically be an isosceles. One of New York’s tallest buildings when it was completed, the Flatiron’s terra-cotta and limestone façade, featuring lion heads and eagles, has been renovated for the reopening, with a specialist employed, the BBC reported, to replicate and restore “thousands of terra-cotta pieces from the facade, reinstalling each by hand”. While the Flatiron might be fondly regarded now, it wasn’t universally popular on its completion, amid fears that the building was so narrow it could fall over. It also didn’t help people warm to the building when it emerged that the design had inadvertently created a “Flatiron breeze” – a powerful, localised wind caused by the building’s shape. According to the author Alice Alexiou, the breeze “blew total strangers into each other’s arms, causing much embarrassment”, and in a tragic incident, blew a 14-year-old messenger boy called John McTaggert into middle of Fifth Avenue, where he was run over by a car and later died. “It was long common knowledge that if you walked by the Flatiron on a windy day, at the very least your skirts were going to end up over your head, and your legs exposed. It was now all the rage for groups of men of a certain character to loiter at the foot of the Flatiron, expressly to catch a glimpse of feminine flesh,” Alexiou wrote in The Flatiron: The New York Landmark and the Incomparable City That Arose with It. Despite the chaos it was causing at street level, the Flatiron defied predictions that it would topple over. “During a 60-mile-an-hour windstorm that battered the city one morning soon after the first tenants moved in, you couldn’t feel the slightest vibration in the building,” Alexiou wrote. It was built to last, in other words, and this latest iteration will continue its legacy – even if its price means it is far beyond the reach of the majority of New Yorkers.

title: D4vd hearing details high hopes and brutal end of girl at heart of murder case
summary: Texts reveal that singer and Celeste Rivas Hernandez had been in touch stretching back to when she was 11 years old
body: The rising pop singer D4vd and 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez were in the throes of a clandestine relationship months before her mangled and decomposing body turned up last September stuffed in an impounded car registered to the musician. D4vd, born David Anthony Burke, is set to stand trial for murder, child sexual abuse and mutilation of human remains in connection to the teenager’s death. Los Angeles county prosecutors accuse Burke of stabbing Celeste to death and subsequently severing her limbs as he sought to prevent her from revealing their sexual relationship, which began when he was 18 and she was 13 in November 2023. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges. The ghastly discovery of Celeste’s remains sent social media sleuths, particularly those in corners of Discord where Burke had carved a niche as an online gamer before pivoting to music, racing through the singer’s past videos and content for any clues concerning his ties to Celeste. The clearest picture yet of a rocky, off-on relationship emerged during a recent preliminary evidentiary hearing, where prosecutors presented text messages that the two exchanged stretching back to 2022, when Celeste was 11. At times, Burke regaled the girl with dreams of an idyllic future: her moving into his home, getting married in Italy and having children together. The fact that she was a minor and had been reported missing by her family, however, cast a shadow over those plans. “i can’t wait to move in tg without the cops bitching baby,” Burke allegedly wrote in June 2024 to her, Courthouse News reported. Months prior, in February, police officers visited him at a residence in West Hollywood after finding his number in the teenager’s phone log as they sought her whereabouts. When police informed Burke of her age, he shared she told him she was 18. Texts indicate that he wanted the sexual nature of their relationship to be a secret. She had asked him in July 2024 if anyone knew they had intercourse. “Nope and I would like to keep it that way before we get married,” Burke replied. Their relationship hit a few rough patches. The teenager expressed a desire for a more serious connection. “All we do is have sex and just hang out man i want more than that for myself,” she reportedly said. In January 2024, after Celeste had become pregnant with Burke’s child, she had an abortion, which she later regretted. “I don’t like talking about it because it gets me really upset, but I’d do anything to have it back,” she reportedly wrote to Burke in August 2024. “Let’s end that there,” he replied. “I don’t like talking to u when you’re upset,” adding later that while the abortion “saddened” him, he did not “dwell on it”. The night before prosecutors say Burke killed Celeste in April 2025, they had a heated argument over text about his relationship with another woman. The teenager allegedly threatened to end his career. Prosecutors had also presented evidence of Burke having a cushy recording label deal, which they suggested gave him motive to allegedly silence Celeste. “What was presented by our office over the course of the last week is a small but illustrative fraction of the evidence investigators have accumulated that proves defendant Burke is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt of the brutal murder of Celeste Rivas Hernandez,” the Los Angeles county district attorney, Nathan J Hochman, said in a statement. “This has been a parent’s worst nightmare, hearing the ghoulish details of how their child was killed, dismembered and left as trash.” It remains unclear what strategy Burke’s attorneys will employ at trial. They did not reply to a request for comment on the case proceeding forward. During the preliminary hearing, the defense team cast doubt on a medical examiner ruling Celeste’s death to be a homicide. Defense attorney Marilyn Bednarski asked Grant Ho, a doctor who performed Celeste’s autopsy, if his report could rule out that the teenager could have been holding an instrument that caused her stab wounds. Ho said he could not, but that the teenager’s autopsy did not indicate self-harm. Prosecutors presented forensic testing that found blood probably originating from Celeste in Burke’s former residence. A second defense attorney, Blair Berk, questioned a Los Angeles police criminalist about why other items in the house were not tested for DNA, noting that multiple people lived in the home. Burke, who remains in custody without bail, will be arraigned in court on 31 August. His trial date has not been announced. Hochman said in a Thursday appearance on NewsNation he will confer with Celeste’s family as well as Burke’s lawyers before deciding whether to pursue the death penalty. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Democrats’ ‘climate hushing’ prompts activists to turn up the volume
summary: Nationwide actions seek to counter view that talking about climate crisis distracts from affordability messaging
body: This summer, torrential rains have washed away Texas neighborhoods, dangerous heat has blanketed swaths of the country, and smoke from Canadian wildfires has choked communities as far south as Florida. Research makes clear that global warming is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe. Yet the climate crisis has largely disappeared from the political agenda, with many Democrats who once described it as an existential threat now shying away from talking about it. Now US activists are pushing back against this trend of “climate hushing”, arguing it is misguided. During the summer’s federal recess, during which lawmakers leave the nation’s capital to work directly within their home states or districts, demonstrators organized by the environmental advocacy coalition Climate Action Campaign are calling on representatives to put climate back on the political agenda. “The long history of the climate movement proves that we move fastest when there’s real pressure from the grassroots,” said Bill McKibben, the environmental author and activist who co-founded climate non-profit 350.org, “All the evidence shows those grassroots are as worried about [the] climate crisis as they ever were.” The events, set to take place over the next month in at least 20 states during the House and Senate recess periods, will mobilize members of groups including local Sierra Club chapters, the senior citizen-led climate organization Third Act, which McKibben founded, and local affiliates of the racial justice group the NAACP. “It’s the broadest brush that we are working with,” said Margie Alt, director of the Climate Action Campaign. “The message is, talk about climate, climate can’t wait, and we want to see action.” Actions began on Thursday and will take a variety of forms. In Michigan, participants will demonstrate against the Republican representative Bill Huizenga who voted for Trump’s so-called big beautiful bill, which boosted planet-heating fossil fuels. In Arizona, young activists will meet with the Democratic representative Adelita Shirley Grijalva, a climate champion, and encourage her to continue talking about global warming. In other districts, organizers have circulated petitions calling on the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, and Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, to prioritize climate issues or plan to call on their representatives to connect the climate crisis to recent heatwaves. The activists’ campaign comes as new polling challenges the need for “climate hushing”, a trend that took off as some policy wonks argued that talking about global warming could alienate voters and distract from the message of affordability. July research from the University of California, Santa Barbara found that emphasizing climate change was neutral to beneficial for Democratic candidates, suggesting that talking more about the issue does not alienate voters and can even increase support in competitive races. Though the Trump administration frequently derides climate policy as a “scam” and a “hoax”, polling indicates most Americans are not onboard with that view. Another July poll from Data for Progress found that 61% of likely voters believe extreme weather has become more frequent over the past five years, including nearly half of Republicans. And one month earlier, a Yale survey found that roughly two-thirds of Americans are worried about global warming. “Smart politicians will grab on this issue,” said McKibben. “There’s perhaps no other question where the gulf between Maga and the general public is higher.” Alt said she saw climate-hushing as “the climate denial of 2026”. “I don’t think that ignoring the climate crisis is smart politics,” she said. “I think that it is dropping the ball on the biggest threat the US and the world faces.”

title: Brazil’s HIV advocates say they predicted USAID funding cuts: ‘We would see the trends’
summary: At the Aids 2026 conference, Brazilian advocates said health systems need to be more independent from foreign funding
body: HIV advocates from Brazil, whose health system operates independently from foreign aid, say they predicted a dramatic reduction in donor funding for HIV and wish other countries had prioritized independence sooner. While the dissolution of USAID might “feel like a rupture”, it’s something advocates at the Brazilian HIV NGO Gestos have seen coming for a long time, Juliana Cesar, Gestos’s political liaison coordinator, said during a session at the Aids 2026 conference in Rio de Janeiro. Brazil is completely independent from foreign assistance for its HIV prevention and treatment programs, as they fall under the purview of Brazil’s Unified Health System. This comparatively robust health system has allowed Brazil to achieve milestones in HIV prevention, including the elimination of HIV transmission to newborns, in 2025. However, negotiations with pharmaceutical companies still limit Brazil’s access to the latest preventions and treatments for HIV, and NIH funding cuts could also curtail HIV related research in Brazil. Cesar explained in an interview that Brazil is in a unique position because the right to healthcare has been enshrined in its constitution since 1988. In the years after the constitution was signed, members of civil society advocated to ensure that HIV prevention and treatment would be part of the Unified Health System. “It has been earmarked into our budgets. We have to make sure that we have enough money for that,” Cesar said. Gestos has advocated for other countries to implement measures similar to Brazil’s Financial Transaction Tax, which took money from every single transaction and put it towards the public health system. But, Cesar explained, the tax was abolished in 2007 as Brazil took a turn toward the right. Cesar also admitted that the tax was not implemented in an ideal way, as the same percentage was imposed on every citizen regardless of income. Cesar has long encouraged other countries to consider measures like this, as it allows them more financial independence from foreign policy whims, and also gives governments more autonomy to tailor HIV programs to their citizens. Cesar first began to suspect that foreign aid would be dramatically reduced more than a decade ago. “We have been tracking negotiations at the UN since the 2000s, and we would see the trends,” Cesar explained. These trends included increasingly restrictive language and conditions around using funding for sexual and reproductive health and rights and for LGBTQ+ communities, both of which are essential for HIV prevention. After 2012, Cesar was increasingly seeing funding “conditions that would exclude the very communities that we should serve”. Different nations would try to find “common ground” surrounding funding, but the common ground “would become stricter and stricter”. Ailish Brennan, a policy analyst at Harm Reduction International, pointed out that foreign aid agreements also frequently require countries to purchase HIV medications from donor countries such as the US. “It’s sort of like pumping money back into the donor country economy,” she said. Domestic production of HIV medications could be “part of a broader shift towards ‘health sovereignty’ and genuine country ownership over health systems”, Brennan added. Countries can also preserve their HIV prevention and treatment programs by redirecting foreign aid that has gone towards “narcotics control”, Brennan noted. A report from Harm Reduction International showed that nearly $1bn worth of foreign aid, including money from USAID, went towards policing and criminalization of narcotics related offenses between 2012 and 2021. Incarceration can, ironically, increase HIV rates as it concentrates high risk populations, including people who inject drugs, and limits their access to healthcare. Brennan pointed out that this money could have instead funded hundreds of thousands of sterile syringes, which help prevent HIV, along with other health measures. Brennan and Anton Basenko, executive director of the International Network of People Who Use Drugs, indicated that HIV prevention funding has long taken advantage of frontline workers’ commitment to their communities. But when organizations deprioritize compensation for on the ground workers, this can also lead to burnout over time. Basenko said that in the wake of the cuts, many HIV prevention organizations “are surviving on the goodwill, unpaid labor, and extraordinary commitment of their staff and volunteers. But resilience should never be mistaken for sustainability.”

title: Why generations swear by hot caldo – ‘a Mexican Gatorade’ – in summer
summary: Across Latin American households in the US, the steaming broth nourishes while keeping family traditions alive
body: When Patty Rodriguez hears the word caldo now, she thinks fondly of home. But as a child growing up in southern California, she despised eating the piping-hot soup-like meal during the summers. Rodriguez would swirl around the chunks of fish with her spoon and imagine that she was performing a magic trick where the dish disappeared. She would roll her eyes as she asked her family why they served the dish more often when it was hot outside. “This is not a hotel,” Rodriguez recalled her mother and aunts saying. “You don’t choose what you want to eat. You’re going to eat what we make.” As an adult, Rodriguez realizes that caldo, which translates to broth in Spanish, was an inexpensive meal that could feed her Mexican American household for several days. It provided the nourishment and hydration needed during the hot summer months. A common dish served throughout Latin America, caldo boasts regional variations in places including Mexico, Puerto Rico and El Salvador. The broth often features whole pieces of meat and chunks of vegetables such as carrots, potatoes and corn on the cob. While the hot meal is served year round, in some cultures it is paradoxically more popular during the summer months. For first- and second-generation Latin Americans, caldo is more than just a meal; it’s a cultural touchstone that connects them to their heritage and helps them honor their families. “Now it’s love,” Rodriguez said as she choked back tears. She’s now the co-founder of Lil’ Libros, a children’s bilingual media company. While working as a radio producer for 20 years, Rodriguez was often the only Latina in her workplace; she yearned to share her culture with her teammates and the audience. Her relationship with caldo evolved as she learned to accept her Mexican American culture. “I was rejecting not just the food,” said Rodriguez, “but I was rejecting my identity.” In recent years, Rodriguez is elated whenever her mother calls to share that she’s made caldo de pollo, which includes pieces of chicken. “I get the kids in the car and I drive to my mom’s house,” Rodriguez said. “I want my children to experience this with her.” Ramon Guzman, a 33-year-old creative director at the Crazy Gorilla and Vezcos Media, still has ambivalent feelings towards caldo. He makes comedy skits on YouTube about Mexican American culture and has poked fun at the dish in several videos over the past decade. In a 2021 video, Guzman imitated a Mexican mother who refused to let her son turn on the air conditioning and forced him to eat caldo as he profusely sweated through his shirt. The skit reflected his childhood growing up as a first-generation Mexican American in San Bernardino, California. “The main emotions were confusion and suffering,” Guzman said, recalling eating caldo as a child. “I did not enjoy eating caldo in the summer. I’m already sweating, and then eating the caldo makes me sweat even more.” Guzman now realizes that the dish provided comfort to his mother, whose family made it for her as a child growing up in Mexico. The dish has followed Guzman into his adulthood; his girlfriend, who is also Mexican American, serves it to him more often during the summer, when she says that she craves it the most. Caldo’s salt and nutrients make it tantamount to “a Mexican Gatorade”, he said. Guzman sees the dish as a tool to teach pain tolerance that has been passed down through generations. He described eating the meal during the summer as “layers and layers of a little pain” that helps people learn to weather the vicissitudes of life. “I will try to dabble in it and make my own version of it whenever I have kids,” Guzman said. “It makes you a bit stronger and more resilient … I’m sure I’m going to be thinking of my mom when I feed it to my future kids.” Caldo is also popular in Puerto Rico. At the San Juan restaurant Cocina al Fondo, chef Natalia Vallejo said that caldo de gallina – a stew that features hen meat, plantains and herbs – is requested by diners more often during the summer. “This dish is deeply connected to my childhood,” she said. “The recipe is inspired by a caldo my paternal grandfather used to make. He cooked it over a wood fire. It’s a dish that evokes memories for Puerto Ricans and brings out many emotions.” Vallejo, who won the James Beard Best Chef: South award in 2023, views caldo as a portal into her past. Her family would use caldo for other recipes. “My favorite memory is that we used the broth to make wood-fired chicken and rice, which was wrapped in banana leaves,” Vallejo said. “It was delicious.” In Aelen Trujillo’s family, caldo served a practical purpose on the hottest days when they wanted to minimize active cooking time. As the dish simmered on the stove, her Mexican grandmother would step away from the warm kitchen so that she wouldn’t overheat. Trujillo, a 24-year-old content creator and stay-at-home mom, now cooks caldo for her family during the summer because it reminds her of her grandmother. She ensures that her young children eat recipes from each of their Mexican and Central American heritages so that they remember their origins. “My grandparents once they came here they had to assimilate and they didn’t have a lot of things. A lot of the culture or the tradition that they had growing up you never really celebrated,” said Trujillo, who is a first-generation Mexican and Honduran American. “Food was the only way that I was able to connect with my culture and feel more Mexican or to touch those roots.”
